notes.meaning: As Jesus walked along after leaving the temple, He noticed a man who had been blind since the day he was born. Unlike other healings in the Gospels where people lost their sight later, this man had never seen anything in his life. Jesus noticed the man's suffering before anyone else brought it up.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine taught that this man born blind represents the whole human race, which is born spiritually blind because of original sin.

notes.meaning: The disciples saw the blind man and wondered what had brought about his condition. In those days, many people assumed that all severe suffering was a direct punishment for a specific evil deed. They asked Jesus whether the man had somehow sinned before birth, or if his parents had sinned to cause his blindness.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that ancient Jewish teachers debated whether an unborn infant could commit sin while still in the womb, which explains the disciples' question.

notes.meaning: Jesus corrected the disciples and rejected both of their ideas. He explained that this blindness did not come from any special fault of the man or his parents. Instead, the man's condition was an occasion for God to put His mighty power and mercy on display.

differ.view: God purposely ordained this man's affliction from the start so that Christ would be glorified through his miraculous healing.
God did not deliberately inflict the disability, but allowed it in His general providence and used the calamity to reveal His grace.

notes.meaning: Jesus told His followers that they had to carry out God's work while there was still daylight to do it. The daytime meant the short season of His earthly ministry before His death. Night meant His coming arrest and death, when His earthly work with them would come to an end.

Jesus declared that as long as He remained on earth, He was the light of the world. Just as the sun brings natural light each day, Jesus brings spiritual truth and life into human darkness. Giving physical sight to the blind man was a living picture of this spiritual truth.

Jesus spat on the ground, mixed the saliva with dust to make mud, and placed it over the blind man's eyes. Saliva was sometimes viewed as an eye remedy in the ancient world, but mud could not heal blindness on its own. By using simple clay, Jesus tested the man's trust and showed His power to work through ordinary things.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early teachers like Augustine saw the clay made from spittle and dust as a symbol of the divine Word taking on human flesh in the Incarnation.

notes.meaning: Jesus commanded the man to go and wash in the Pool of Siloam, a name that means 'Sent.' The water itself held no special power, but the man proved his trust by obeying the command. As soon as he washed the mud away, he received his sight and returned seeing clearly.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching views the washing in the Pool of Siloam as a symbol of baptism, which washes away sin and gives spiritual sight.

notes.meaning: Neighbors and people who had frequently seen the man begging noticed an astonishing difference in him. He had been a familiar beggar sitting day after day along the roadside. Now that he could see and walk freely, they began asking if he really was the same person.

The onlookers began to argue about the man's identity. Some were sure he was the beggar, but others thought he only looked like him because his opened eyes gave his face a brand-new expression. The man ended the debate himself by speaking up and telling them that he was indeed the beggar.

Once the crowd realized he was truly the same man, they wanted to understand what had taken place. They knew that a person born blind could never naturally gain the power of sight. Their question showed their amazement and their desire to know how this impossible cure had been done.

The man gave a simple and direct report of what had happened to him. He explained that a man called Jesus made mud, put it on his eyes, and sent him to wash at the pool of Siloam. When he followed those directions, his sight was granted immediately.

The people asked where Jesus had gone, wanting to find Him for themselves. The healed man honestly answered that he did not know. Because he had been blind when Jesus spoke to him and had walked away to the pool, he had never seen the Lord with his own eyes.

The crowd led the healed man to the Pharisees, who were respected religious leaders and experts in the law. The community looked to these teachers to settle difficult religious questions. They wanted the Pharisees to examine the miracle and decide whether it was lawful.

John points out that Jesus made the mud and gave the man sight on the Sabbath, the Jewish day of rest. Man-made traditions of that day strictly banned kneading dough or making mud on the Sabbath, and applying medicine was also forbidden. By healing on that day, Jesus openly set aside those human rules.

The Pharisees questioned the man again, demanding to know how he had gained his sight. The man did not change his account, giving them the same plain summary he gave his neighbors earlier. He declared that Jesus put mud on his eyes, he washed it off, and now he could see.

The religious leaders split into two opposing camps over the news. Some argued that Jesus could not be sent from God because He did not keep their strict rules about the Sabbath. Others asked how an evil impostor could ever perform such remarkable, miraculous signs.

Because the Pharisees could not agree among themselves, they asked the healed man for his own opinion about Jesus. They wanted to know what conclusion he had reached after receiving such a miracle. The man boldly answered that Jesus was a prophet, a messenger who truly spoke and acted for God.

The hostile Jewish leaders refused to believe that the man had ever been blind at all. Accepting the miracle would mean admitting that God had worked through Jesus, which they were unwilling to do. To see if the family had invented a trick, they summoned the man's parents for questioning.

The leaders pressed the parents with three sharp questions at once. They asked if the man was their son, if they truly claimed he was born blind, and how it was that he could now see. They hoped the parents would contradict their son and prove the miracle was a fraud.

The parents answered the first two questions plainly and without any doubt. They confirmed that the man was indeed their son and that he had been blind from the day of his birth. Their testimony completely ruined the leaders' attempt to claim the disability had been faked.
